name: Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy
aliases: corneal dystrophy of Bowman layer type 1

reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / corneal dystrophy literature
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant dystrophy affecting the Bowman layer, associated with mutations in the TGFBI gene
Presents in childhood with recurrent painful corneal erosions
Progressive superficial opacities develop at the level of Bowman layer, reducing vision over time
It shares its TGFBI genetic basis with other classic stromal dystrophies (granular, lattice, Thiel-Behnke)
Erosions tend to lessen with age as opacification and scarring increase
It commonly recurs in grafts after keratoplasty, so superficial ablative procedures are often preferred
reference.pathophysiology: Reis-Bucklers corneal dystrophy is caused by mutations in the transforming growth factor beta-induced (TGFBI) gene, leading to deposition of abnormal protein at the level of the Bowman layer and superficial stroma. The abnormal material disrupts and replaces the Bowman layer, causing surface irregularity, poor epithelial adhesion with recurrent erosions in early life, and progressive superficial opacification that degrades vision. Because the underlying epithelial and anterior stromal cells continue to produce the abnormal protein, the dystrophy characteristically recurs in corneal grafts.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior corneal scarring from other cause
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of the superficial opacities
TGFBI genetic testing to confirm and subtype
Corneal topography and imaging (for example anterior segment OCT)
Family history and examination of relatives
Assessment of visual impact and erosion frequency
reference.prognosis: Vision declines gradually with superficial opacification; superficial keratectomy or phototherapeutic ablation can improve vision, though the dystrophy tends to recur, including in grafts.
pitfalls: Confusing it with Thiel-Behnke or other TGFBI dystrophies without genetic testing
Performing penetrating keratoplasty when a superficial procedure would avoid rapid recurrence
Overlooking the autosomal dominant family history
management: Treat recurrent corneal erosions with intensive ocular lubricants, hyperosmotic agents and a bandage soft contact lens during acute episodes
Phototherapeutic keratectomy or superficial keratectomy to remove abnormal Bowman-layer deposits and improve both surface irregularity and vision
Prefer superficial ablative procedures over penetrating keratoplasty because the TGFBI-driven deposits characteristically recur within grafts
Topical antibiotic cover for epithelial defects and analgesia for the pain of acute erosions
Regular slit-lamp and topographic monitoring to track opacification, erosion frequency and visual decline
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant TGFBI dystrophy, with examination and testing of at-risk relatives
Refer to a corneal specialist for surgical planning and consideration of repeat superficial ablation when disease recurs
